p: **Series:** the same current flows through each resistor, and the pds add up. **R_{S} = R₁ + R₂ + R₃**.
**Parallel:** every branch has the same pd, and the branch currents add. **1/R_{P} = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃**.
R_{P} is always smaller than the smallest branch.

rules: The **ammeter** is in series and has about 0 Ω.
The **voltmeter** is in parallel and has a very high resistance.
An **open switch** can have a pd across it. Here no current flows anywhere, so V₂ shows the supply pd and V₁ shows 0.
An ammeter in a voltmeter’s place is a **short circuit**: it bypasses the part.

screens.q: A 9 V battery with negligible internal resistance, a switch S, a 4 Ω resistor and an 8 Ω resistor are connected in series with an ammeter A. Voltmeter V₁ is across the 8 Ω resistor. Voltmeter V₂ is across S. The meters are ideal. (a) S is open. Write down the reading on V₁ and on V₂, and explain each. (4) (b) S is closed. Calculate the reading on the ammeter. (3) (c) Calculate the reading on V₁, and write down the reading on V₂. (3)

lines.x: 0 V ✓. No current flows, so there is no pd across the 8 Ω (V = IR = 0) ✓.

ask.prompt: S is open. What does V₁ read?

traps: No current flows, so the 8 Ω has no pd across it: V = IR = 0.
That is V₁ when S is closed. With S open, no current flows.

lines.x: 9 V ✓. With no current the resistors have no pd, so the whole 9 V is across the gap ✓.

ask.prompt: S is open. What does V₂ read?

traps: This is the trap in the Examiners’ Report 2019. With no current, the resistors have no pd, so the whole 9 V is across the gap.

ask.prompt: S is closed. Work out the ammeter reading.

traps: That uses the 4 Ω only. The current goes through both: R_{S} = 12 Ω.
That uses the 8 Ω only. R_{S} = 4 + 8 = 12 Ω.
That is the pd across the 4 Ω. V₁ is across the 8 Ω.
Now a current flows, so the 4 Ω takes part of the 9 V.

lines.x: 0 V, because a closed switch has no resistance ✓
